source.title: Towards Understanding the Regularization of Adversarial Robustness on Neural Networks
source.authors: Yu-Xin Wen; Shuai Li; K. Jia

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present, including appendices.
record.tranche_reason: The paper reports that stronger adversarial training increases training loss and reduces training accuracy, showing that robustness regularization can limit fitting. This refines the broad training claim, though it does not test the claim's random-initialization or zero-error conditions directly.
record.gate_note: The paper tests adversarial training strength and reports training accuracy and loss alongside test results. Singular-value and margin-distribution results are discussed, but exact per-condition values are shown in figures without textual numeric descriptions, so they are not recorded as rows. PGD attack results measure adversarial accuracy rather than the claimed training behavior.
record.test_reason: The study reports clean training classification accuracy for convolutional networks trained with momentum SGD on CIFAR-10/100 under adversarial regularization. These results bear on V1's fitting and regularized-recipe clauses in a new training setting. They do not test the other versions merely by using Fixup initialization or omitting batch normalization.
record.authors_conclusion: The record broadly captures the authors' conclusion: adversarial training smooths feature changes, concentrates margins near decision boundaries, reduces confidence and surrogate-loss generalization gaps, and degrades standard test accuracy. Qualify the gap statement: classification-error gaps increase on high-capacity CIFAR-10 runs. The authors also argue that sufficient capacity can preserve training-set overfitting despite adversarial regularization.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses adversarially augmented PGD or FGSM training to investigate robustness regularization; it does not test the ordinary random-initialization training recipes in the claim versions.
record.method_sensitivity: Training accuracy declines as adversarial defensive strength increases; outcomes are reported across datasets and network sizes. The CIFAR-10 error-rate gap can increase with AR for large-capacity models, while loss gaps decrease; spectral normalization changes the error-gap trend.

fits_no_version.finding: Tiny-ImageNet clean training accuracy declines from 79.12% without adversarial training to 60.73% at strength 16.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Adversarial training can reduce clean training-set fitting on Tiny-ImageNet.

fits_no_version.finding: FGSM training reduces standard test accuracy as defensive strength increases.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Stronger FGSM adversarial training can reduce standard test accuracy on CIFAR-10/100.

fits_no_version.finding: Stronger adversarial training concentrates margins around zero and reduces singular-value dispersion in most layers.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Adversarial training smooths feature responses and reduces prediction confidence; these measurements do not test initialization-dependent optimization.

record.peer_reviewed: International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 119, 2020
record.problems: No standard-training comparison is provided for the training-accuracy results in the raw tables. The central claim versions concern ordinary gradient training, initialization, width, depth, learning rate, or batch normalization; the paper instead studies adversarial regularization. Many margin and singular-value findings are plotted without exact tabulated values. The FGSM table does not report training accuracy.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted. PGD attack accuracy values were excluded because they measure adversarial test accuracy, not training classification error. Singular-value and margin-distribution plots have no precise numeric text values to assign.

untested.parts: Random or corrupted labels, Adam, early stopping, and an ordinary-training CIFAR control are not tested. Random weight initialization is not explicitly documented for the CIFAR runs. The model comparison varies depth rather than systematically locating a sufficient-size threshold.
No two-layer ReLU teacher-student experiment, spurious-minimum frequency, or extra-neuron comparison.
No comparison of plain and residual networks across depth, longer-training control, or test of very deep plain tanh networks.
No initialization comparison measuring training speed, signal propagation, or trainable depth.
No learning-rate stability threshold, curvature trajectory, catapult recovery, or edge-of-stability measurement.
No matched comparison of training speed, stability, or tolerated learning rates with and without batch normalization. Fixup is used as an implementation tool.

missing.what: Nine additional training-accuracy conditions for spectrally normalized ResNet-56 on CIFAR-10: spectral caps 1, 3 and 5, each at PGD strengths 4/8/16. Accuracies are respectively 96.91/94.38/90.58%, 99.65/98.51/95.94%, and 99.57/98.33/95.96%. The uncontrolled conditions duplicate R1–R3. These results directly characterize fitting under additional regularization and were not declared omitted.

record.verdict_notes: CIFAR models use momentum SGD and Fixup-based initialization without batch normalization or Fixup scalar layers; the main runs omit spectral normalization. Tiny-ImageNet retains batch normalization. Training accuracy is evaluated on natural examples. Higher training loss or lower confidence alone does not establish failure to achieve near-zero classification error. No results warrant a challenge to V1's ordinary-training claim.

versions.untested_parts: Does not test random or corrupted labels, Adam, early stopping, or a comparison of model sizes under standard training; tests adversarially trained ResNets and a Wide ResNet on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and Tiny-ImageNet.

source_check.notes: Training errors are calculated as 100% minus tabled accuracy; defensive strengths 4/8/16 mean perturbation bounds 4/255, 8/255 and 16/255. Appendix B.5 reports variability across examples for loss variation, but Tables 3–4 provide no training-accuracy uncertainty estimates.

statements.correction: Table 3: ResNet-56 training errors 1.55% and 4.03% at strengths 8 and 16; ResNet-110 training error 1.58% at strength 16. Weaker conditions yield 0.49%, 0.05% and 0.38% error. These results support V1's stated recipe dependence.
statements.problem: The CIFAR-10 numbers and condition dependence are correct, but the limits_scope classification treats V1's explicit regularized-recipe qualification as a new limitation.

reader_labels.condition: PGD adversarially trained ResNet-56 and ResNet-110 on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100, and Wide ResNet on Tiny-ImageNet
reader_labels.reason: Training accuracy is below 100% throughout and decreases with greater defensive strength in the listed CIFAR and Tiny-ImageNet runs (R1–R16), so adversarial robustness can limit fitting. These results do not directly test ordinary random-initialized training or zero-error behavior under the version's stated recipes.
